added_claim_errors: "If the money lands in January, it generally counts for 2027, and the 2026 room is lost": wrong per key; the 2026 Form 5498 instructions and 219(f)(3) allow a rollover designated for 2026 through April 15, 2027 (whether the plan processes it that way varies by plan), so December 31 is not the federal deadline
"If annual limits rise, it could take fewer years": contradicts key; even at $8,000 x 4 = $32,000 < $35,000, the full $35,000 still takes at least five tax years

"Finish by December 31, 2026 so it counts against the 2026 limit": treats December as the deadline; key says a rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027 (plan-dependent), so this is a minor error

"If you contributed in 2021-2026, that money isn't eligible": too broad; the lookback is the 5 years before the transfer date, so 2021 contributions made more than 5 years before a late-2026 transfer do qualify

reasons: Both answers open by correcting the premise. Both give the $7,500 annual cap tied to earned income, the $35,000 lifetime cap, the $13,000 that can never move, a son-owned Roth and a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer, and a state-tax caveat. Both wrongly treat December 31 as the federal deadline. A is more emphatic about it ("the 2026 room is lost") and also says rising limits "could take fewer years", which contradicts the five-year minimum. B also says Roth income limits do not apply, conditions the 15-year test on the beneficiary never having changed, and names the 6% excise and the earnings-plus-10% consequences of an improper move. A never covers those consequences. A gives more operational detail (partial-rollover check, acceptance letters, IRS sources), but B's coverage is more complete and a bit tighter, so B wins narrowly.
